visible.summary:
In August 2026 the Kelantan assembly passed a new Syariah Criminal Offences Bill — including a clause making gender change an offence for persons under the state's syariah jurisdiction — replacing provisions of the state's 2019 syariah criminal code that Malaysia's Federal Court had struck down as outside state power. The Bill also carries "protection of modesty" decency offences, backed by whipping (3–6 strokes), fines up to RM5,000 and imprisonment up to three years.

The sequence — invalidation by the federal courts, prompt deliberate re-enactment by the state assembly — documents institutional determination to criminalise gender transition, not a stray provision. The gender-change offence binds Muslims, including Muslim travellers exposed to syariah proceedings; the official climate it signals reaches all trans visitors.
visible.tangentialFactors: The same 2026 Bill's 'protection of modesty' provisions criminalise general moral and decency conduct for Muslims beyond gender transition — broad syariah policing that reaches same-sex conduct and gender presentation as a category, not trans status alone.

sources.claim: Kelantan's newly passed Syariah Criminal Offences (Kelantan) Bill 2026 (passed Aug 2026) contains provisions on covering aurat (modesty), gender change, and safeguarding the modesty of private parts, replacing 16 provisions of the Kelantan Syariah Criminal Code Enactment 2019 struck down by the Federal Court. Clause 15 mandates Muslims safeguard the sanctity and modesty of their private parts in accordance with Islamic law. For this record: the state's legislative direction explicitly regulates gender-change matters under Islamic criminal law, with enforcement beginning 2026.

Follow-up report confirms Kelantan passed strict new decency rules via the Syariah Criminal Offences (Kelantan) Bill 2026 (13 Aug 2026), legislating decency, aurat-covering, and gender-change provisions; the enactment replaces 16 provisions of the 2019 enactment struck down by the Federal Court. The article also notes a related Feb 2026 first Kelantan Syariah Court case involving gender change. For this record: confirms the new decency/gender-change legislation is now in force and being applied by the Syariah courts.

visible.summary: The most concentrated wave of mob violence against transgender women in Indonesia: ten attacks on 45 victim-survivors in Bogor between 30 March and 15 July 2026, documented by Pelangi Nusantara — groups of 10–20 men punched, kicked, threw stones, glass bottles and firecrackers at trans women and stripped some of them naked, filming the assaults for social media under the account @bogorbersihlgbt ('Bogor clean of LGBT'). No alleged perpetrator has been publicly identified, arrested or prosecuted; a trans-rights activist who accompanied women filing police reports said officers 'accepted the case but worked on it half-heartedly,' and some survivors were too afraid to report. Separately, on 22 June 2025 police detained 75 people at a villa raid in the Puncak area of Bogor Regency at a gathering labelled a 'gay party' that violated no law — Amnesty demanded their release. Activists attribute the violence's legitimisation to Perpres 111/2025, which from October 2025 lists 'LGBTQ culture' as a national-resilience threat alongside terrorism and drug abuse: 'people feel able to commit violence arbitrarily because they believe the state has legitimised that violence.' The pattern-plus-impunity combination is West Java-specific; national same-sex criminalisation does not by itself explain the street-vigilante wave with total state inaction and explicit anti-trans branding over four months.
visible.tangentialFactors: The 22 June 2025 Puncak villa mass detention (75 people) targeted a gay gathering rather than gender identity — same-sex-conduct policing that nonetheless shows the Bogor/West Java security apparatus actively mass-proceeds against LGBT people as a category.

sources.claim: ABC News (15 Aug 2026): men doused a trans woman with what looked like urine on a street in Bogor, West Java, one of a wave of attacks; activists link the violence to a 2025 presidential regulation classifying the 'spread of LGBTQ culture' as a non-military threat plus discriminatory regional regulations, saying the state's language legitimises violence against trans women. A trans woman quoted says those who previously appeared in public now live in fear. For this record: documents street violence against trans women within the region and the national regulatory backdrop enabling it.

Tempo (25-26 June 2025): Indonesian police detained 75 people at a villa in Puncak, Bogor Regency, West Java, at a gathering police called an LGBT 'family gathering' held 'to avoid detection'; West Java Regional Police confirmed the June 22, 2025 arrests, which followed a tip from local residents. For this record: a concrete 2025 enforcement action against an LGBT gathering inside the region, showing police actively investigate and detain LGBT gatherings in West Java.

Amnesty International (24 June 2025) condemned the arrest of 75 people in the raid on a privately rented villa in Puncak, Bogor, West Java, calling it a discriminatory raid and 'a blatant violation of human rights and privacy' exemplifying the hostile environment for LGBTI people in Indonesia; Amnesty said the gathering violated no law and demanded release and accountability. For this record: international framing of the West Java raid as unlawful, reinforcing that LGBTI gatherings in the region face police action despite violating no law.

visible.summary:
The clearest enacted modern local anti-LGBT bylaw outside Aceh: Bukittinggi City Regional Regulation (Perda) No. 2 of 2024 on public order, articles 43-44, prescribes oral and written warnings, cessation of activities, social rehabilitation programmes, and administrative fines of Rp1,000,000 targeting LGBT people. Enforcement is real but contested: a 2026 field study of the Perda's implementation reports supervision, enforcement and guidance by the local order force (Satpol PP), with sanctions of suboptimal effectiveness and rehabilitation hampered because the facilities barely exist; a 2025 study records people recorded as swept up in LGBT sweeps/app findings jumping from 56 in 2023 to 272 in 2024, and customary-law actors pushing parallel measures (a boarding-house barcode system, proposed nagari regulations on social deviance). Limapuluh Kota regency finalised a draft (ranperda, articles 13-14) on public tranquility containing an explicit LGBT prohibition with administrative fines in the tens of millions of rupiah plus mandated "rehabilitation" (psychosocial counselling, spiritual guidance, resocialisation) for people of same-sex attraction. OutRight's Creeping Criminalisation mapping of discriminatory regional regulations covers eight other provinces (not West Sumatra itself, whose key bylaws postdate the study), but documents the same regional-autonomy mechanism this province's bylaws instantiate.

This sits below the national score because an enacted bylaw with specified sanctions creates visitor-facing risk (detention, forced rehabilitation programmes, fines) that does not exist in most provinces; the documented apprehension counts show the bylaw environment is actively policed, though no caning (an Aceh-specific penalty) or prosecution under these provisions is recorded. It remains above West Java (0.06), where patterned mob violence with zero accountability is the primary threat, and above the national floor where no such bylaw exists at all.
visible.tangentialFactors: The Bukittinggi Perda and Limapuluh Kota draft target LGBT people broadly (same-sex conduct framing); the direct trans-specific element is the "rehabilitation"/gender-normative enforcement layer and Satpol PP profiling of gender-nonconforming people.
visible.localsOnly: Social rehabilitation programmes, boarding-house barcode registration and nagari-level customary sanctions operate on residents; visitors are exposed mainly to sweep/apprehension risk.

sources.claim: Academic article (AHKAM journal) analysing Bukittinggi City (West Sumatra) Regional Regulation (Perda) No. 2 of 2024 on Public Order targeting LGBT, examined from the perspective of Fiqih Siyasah Tanfidziyah (implementation of Islamic governance): the regulation is framed as responding to local religious values and Minangkabau customs. For this record: documents a 2024 local anti-LGBT public-order regulation in a West Sumatra city, showing formal municipal-level restrictions.

Peer-reviewed study (2025) of LGBT cases in Bukittinggi City, West Sumatra: recorded cases rose from 56 individuals in 2023 to 272 in 2024; the Kurai Customary Law Community (Masyarakat Hukum Adat Kurai) acts as a non-state actor, initiating the customary sanction 'dibuang sepanjang adat' (expulsion under adat), proposing village regulations on social deviance, and implementing barcode monitoring in boarding houses to police LGBT presence. For this record: documents rising state-and-adat surveillance and customary sanctions against LGBT people within a West Sumatra city.

Mimbarsumbar.id (13 May 2026): the DPRD (regional legislature) of Limapuluh Kota regency, West Sumatra, finalised a draft anti-LGBT regional regulation (Ranperda) within a Public Order and Tranquility (Trantibum) regulation, including administrative fines and rehabilitation for LGBT people; the drafting body chair stated stages have reached finalisation. For this record: a 2026 draft provincial-level regulation introducing fines and 'rehabilitation' targeting LGBT people in a West Sumatra regency.

OutRight Action International, 'Creeping Criminalisation' (Katjasungkana & Wieringa; cached copy): maps discriminatory national laws and regional regulations across eight Indonesian provinces (Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatra, South Sulawesi, South Sumatra, Yogyakarta) - the reference for Indonesia's regional-bylaw mechanism; West Sumatra's newer Bukittinggi regulation postdates the mapping.

visible.summary:
Bali is Indonesia's most tolerant mainstream environment: 2026 travel guidance still describes a "live and let live" ethos, with gay-friendly life concentrated in Seminyak, Canggu and Ubud, and no criminal enforcement against foreign tourists recorded. That informality, however, is not protection. The national penal code brought into force in 2026 criminalises extramarital sex, including same-sex relations; LGBTQ+ travel advisories rate the island "Exercise Significant Caution", public displays of affection are discouraged for all couples, and same-sex marriage remains unrecognised.

A 2025 ethnographic study of the island's trans women (transpuan) communities pointedly challenges the "refuge" framing, documenting persistent misrecognition and systemic discrimination beneath the tolerant surface. Visitors should read Bali as relatively safer by local custom — with the new penal code, conservative local administration and documented structural discrimination setting the limits of that safety.
visible.tangentialFactors: Same-sex conduct provisions (KUHP Art. 412 cohabitation/sex outside marriage) reach trans visitors in couples or shared accommodation, complaint-based but newly available as a leverage tool in any police contact.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Bali's general tourism-hazard profile (traffic, surf, scams) is unrelated to trans risk; the island's relative safety is a social-fact, not a legal exemption.

sources.claim: Peer-reviewed article (Anthropology of the Middle East, 2025) on the 'precarious lives' of the transpuan (trans feminine) community in Indonesia based on four ethnographic case studies in Bali: documents how transpuan people navigate circumstances marked by both resistance and misrecognition and discrimination, challenging the narrative of victimhood while showing real precarity. For this record: academic ground-truth that Bali hosts a visible trans community living with precarity, discrimination, and informal resistance.

Travel guide (Gayborhood/Traven) on Bali: ranks the destination '6.3/10' with a legal score of 2.0, warning same-sex relations are criminalised in Indonesia and that LGBTQ+ travellers face legal risks; advises visitors to 'keep your love a little quieter' despite the island's tolerant reputation. For this record: practical traveller-facing warning that Bali's legal backdrop (Indonesian national law) carries criminalisation risk even where the local scene is accepting.

Travel guide (Mar 2026): Bali is broadly welcoming to LGBTQ+ travellers on a 'live and let live' basis, and same-sex relationships are not a criminal offence in Bali under Indonesian national law, though the new Criminal Code (KUHP, in effect Jan 2026) adds complexity; same-sex marriage is not legally recognised anywhere in Indonesia; Seminyak (Eat Street/Batu Belig), Canggu and Ubud are named as the most consistently LGBTQ+-friendly areas with active venues, while public displays of affection warrant discretion. For this record: current, specific traveller guidance for trans/LGBTQ visitors to Bali including the 2026 KUHP law change.

visible.summary:
No trans-specific legal measure or incident series is documented for this province in the surviving sources. The security environment, however, is not neutral: rights monitors recorded 138 acts of torture or ill-treatment in detention by police and military in the highland conflict zones of the island's western half between September 2021 and early 2025, "with almost no consequences", and a further surge of military deployments, fatal shootings and arbitrary detentions from August 2025, alongside internal displacement.

For any visitor — including a transgender one — contact with security forces in the highland districts carries a documented risk of arbitrary detention and mistreatment, and the surveillance environment raises the chance of being noticed and questioned. This is a general-population security finding, not evidence of trans-specific targeting.
visible.tangentialFactors: The new national KUHP (Jan 2026) applies fully in Papua; the region-specific factor is not an anti-LGBT bylaw (none found) but a documented security-force abuse pattern that worsens any police contact, including for gender-nonconforming travellers.

sources.claim: TAPOL briefing (July 2025): police and military in West Papua committed 138 recorded acts of torture or ill-treatment in detention in Maybrat and the Central Highlands (Sept 2021-Q1 2025) with almost no consequences; victims mostly males under 24 plus 7 women and 7 minors; arrests largely for alleged armed-group links or demonstrations; deaths during torture documented in operation areas; incidents catalogued on the 'Papuans Behind Bars' database.

Human Rights Monitor Papua Quarterly Report Q3 2025 (31 Oct 2025) on West Papua: documents killings, arbitrary detentions, torture and the failure of accountability mechanisms by security forces expanding across the territory, plus a healthcare crisis under scrutiny and arrests of protesters. Contains no trans/LGBTI-specific findings. For this record: indicates a high-violence, low-accountability security climate in West Papua relevant to overall traveller safety, but provides no trans-specific substance.

Since June 2021 Indonesia's Ministry of Home Affairs has run outreach issuing transgender Indonesians identification papers (KTP), and the page names Papua among the provinces whose trans residents have benefited (with Banten, West Java, Central Java, East Java, North Sumatra, South Sumatra, South Sulawesi and Lampung); only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors are recognised, with birth-gender printed unless a court order was already obtained. The same page's national-framework facts apply in Papua: the 2022 penal-code amendment criminalising sexual activity outside marriage (up to one year in prison) takes effect on 2 January 2026, same-sex marriage is not recognised, and customary laws may apply. For this record: evidence that trans people in Papua may obtain identity documents through the national outreach programme, and the national legal framework a trans visitor stands under while in the province.

visible.summary:
In April 2025 Makassar's mayor Munafri 'Appi' Arifuddin reaffirmed his commitment to pushing through an anti-LGBT Perda after a same-sex act at a night entertainment venue went viral; the deputy chair of the DPRD's legislation body, Anwar Faruq, backed it as urgently needed "to preserve moral order and religious norms." South Sulawesi is one of the eight provinces analysed in OutRight International's discriminatory-regulation mapping. No enacted local bylaw with specified penalties yet exists in the province, and no violence wave or mass police raid against trans people is documented in the dossier.

The small negative deviation from the national score reflects an active legislative push in a major domestic-tourism gateway to eastern Indonesia, raising the probability of future discriminatory enforcement. It remains above West Sumatra (0.11), where a Perda with articles specifying fines and rehabilitation is already on the books, and above Jakarta (0.12), where a 56-person raid without legal basis has already occurred: the law here is proposed, not enacted, and per the enforcement-over-statute rule the traveler-facing impact is prospective.
visible.tangentialFactors: The proposed Perda targets LGBT people broadly; its practical exposure for trans visitors would run through the same Satpol PP moral-order enforcement used in other South Sulawesi cities, if enacted.

sources.claim: Harian.News (27 Apr 2025): the Mayor of Makassar (South Sulawesi) reaffirmed commitment to pushing an anti-LGBT regional regulation (Perda) after a same-sex act at a night-entertainment venue went viral; the deputy chair of the DPRD Makassar law-drafting body (Bapemperda) voiced support, saying such a regulation is needed to preserve moral and religious norms. For this record: documents formal municipal push in Makassar toward an anti-LGBT regulation in 2025.

OutRight Action International, 'Creeping Criminalisation' (Katjasungkana & Wieringa): maps discriminatory national laws and regional regulations in eight Indonesian provinces - South Sulawesi among them - documenting how provincial and city bylaws criminalise same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity under regional autonomy.

Merdeka (25 April 2026, sourced from Antara) reports that the Makassar city government's women's-empowerment and child-protection agency (DP3A) is intensifying LGBT 'prevention' through socialization and education aimed at school-age children plus case handling, with counselling and a safe house for reported individuals, in response to community reports. DP3A head Ita Isdiana Anwar says most reports come from worried families, and DPRD Kota Makassar member Muchlis Misbah, citing a Komisi D monitoring meeting showing rising LGBT numbers alongside HIV/AIDS cases, backs the pending Ranperda on HIV/AIDS and LGBT as legal reinforcement. This is a dated, Makassar-city-specific record of the administrative track of the anti-LGBT push the record describes, confirming that as of April 2026 the local rule remains proposed (Ranperda) rather than enacted.

Tribun News' republication of a BBC News Indonesia report (10 January 2023, reporting by Muhammad Aidil) states that Makassar's anti-LGBT raperda had entered the 2023 local legislative programme (prolegda) as a 'priority for discussion', with two DPRD Makassar members, including PKS-faction member Azwar ST, saying the proposal models itself on Perda already passed elsewhere such as Bogor. Constitutional-law expert Bivitri Susanti calls such raperdas a 'trend ahead of the political year' that risks worsening discrimination and persecution of LGBT people, and notes the central government does little to stop discriminatory local regulations. This verifies Makassar as a recurring site of the anti-LGBT bylaw push since at least early 2023, predating the April 2025 mayoral reaffirmation the record cites, and consistent with its 'proposed, not enacted' status.
